items.title: Sour Tastes Hijack the Tongue to Mute Sweetness, Bitterness, and Saltiness
items.snippet: Why does a sour bite overpower sweet, salty, and bitter flavors? A new study reveals that taste buds act as miniature processing hubs, releasing serotonin in response to sourness to mute competing flavors before signals ever reach the brain.

items.title: Older Brains Lose Synchronization Between Movement and Body Temperature
items.snippet: Even when 24-hour circadian rhythms persist into old age, faster multi-hour "ultradian" rhythms weaken significantly. New research shows aging decouples physical activity from core body temperature while triggering immune gene activation and neuronal loss inside the brain's master clock.

items.title: Scent and Memory: Why Novelty Boosts Recall in Older Adults
items.snippet: Can diffusing lavender really sharpen your memory? A new study reveals that scent alone doesn't boost recall, unless older adults experience it as a novel sensory cue at the very beginning of learning.

items.title: How ADHD Shapes Breathing and Time Perception
items.snippet: ADHD reaches far beyond inattention and hyperactivity. New studies reveal that the condition alters breathing patterns, triggers chronic time pressure, lowers regional brain iron in youth, and influences problem drinking in young adults.

items.title: How Lead Exposure Erodes Long-Term Memory
items.snippet: How does environmental lead exposure erode memory? Researchers found lead disrupts oxidation-reduction balance inside neuronal mitochondria, shutting down the new protein synthesis required to lock in long-term memories.

items.title: New wearable ultrasound patch boosts REM sleep without drugs or surgery
items.snippet: A revolutionary new wearable patch could help people get more restorative sleep without medication or surgery. Developed by University of Texas researchers, the device uses gentle ultrasound to stimulate deep brain regions, helping participants enter REM sleep 43 minutes faster and remain there 16 minutes longer on average. items.title: A hidden biological divide may help explain Alzheimer’s and chronic pain
items.snippet: New research reveals that biological sex, genetics, and menopause may dramatically influence Alzheimer's risk, treatment responses, and chronic pain conditions such as fibromyalgia. Scientists also uncovered surprising differences in immune activity and gut-brain interactions, opening the door to more personalized treatments for neurological disorders.

items.title: MIT scientists discover a surprising way to boost the brain’s nighttime cleaning system
items.snippet: MIT scientists discovered that carefully timed bursts of gentle pink noise during sleep can strengthen the brain’s natural cleaning waves, which help flush away potentially harmful waste. The breakthrough could pave the way for new treatments aimed at improving sleep and memory while potentially reducing the buildup of proteins linked to Alzheimer’s disease.

items.title: An ancient virus may help explain what makes the human brain different
items.snippet: A virus that infected chimpanzees millions of years ago may have helped shape one of the most important differences between humans and our closest relatives: how our brains develop. items.title: Scientists discover that the heart doesn't age the way we thought
items.snippet: Scientists have discovered that the heart ages unevenly, with surprising hotspots of inflammation and scarring concentrated in the valves and major blood vessels rather than the heart muscle. The findings challenge long-standing assumptions about cardiac aging and could help researchers develop new ways to protect the heart as we grow older.
